subject: chemistry-hl
about: Original practice questions written for the IB Chemistry 2025 guide (HL). Not IB past-paper questions or markschemes, and not a prediction of exam questions. Data-based practice; a calculator is allowed.

items.topicLabel: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
items.stem:
Data: Heating curve data: a solid is heated at a constant rate. Temperature (°C) every minute: 20, 41, 62, 80, 80, 80, 80, 95, 110.

State the melting point and explain the shape between minutes 3 and 6.
markscheme: Melting point = 80 °C (1)
Between minutes 3 and 6 the solid is melting: the energy supplied overcomes attractions between particles, so average kinetic energy (temperature) does not rise (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.stem:
Data: Mass spectrum of element Q: m/z 69, relative abundance 60; m/z 71, relative abundance 40.

Calculate Ar(Q) and use the data booklet to identify Q.
markscheme: Q is gallium (closest Ar in the data booklet) (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.stem:
Data: Successive ionization energies of element R (kJ mol⁻¹): 1st 578, 2nd 1817, 3rd 2745, 4th 11577, 5th 14842.

Plot or inspect log(IE) against electrons removed. Deduce the group and give the condensed configuration if R is in period 3.
markscheme: Large jump between the 3rd and 4th ionization energies, so 3 valence electrons: group 13 (1)
Period 3: aluminium, [Ne]3s²3p¹ (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
items.stem:
Data: Heating hydrated copper(II) sulfate. Crucible 20.00 g; crucible + hydrated salt 22.50 g; crucible after heating to constant mass 21.60 g. M(CuSO₄) = 159.62, M(H₂O) = 18.02.

Determine x in CuSO₄·xH₂O and suggest why heating to constant mass matters.
markscheme: Ratio ≈ 1 : 5, so x = 5 (1)
Heating to constant mass shows all the water has been removed; otherwise x comes out too low (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.stem:
Data: Pressure–volume data for a gas at constant temperature: P/kPa 50, 100, 200, 400; V/cm³ 96, 48, 24, 12.

Show the data fit the ideal model and state the graph that gives a straight line.
markscheme: P × V = 4800 kPa cm³ for every pair, so V ∝ 1/P at constant temperature, as the ideal gas model predicts (1)
A graph of V against 1/P (or P against 1/V) is a straight line through the origin (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.stem:
Data: Lattice enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹, booklet): NaF 930, NaCl 790, NaBr 754, NaI 705; MgCl₂ 2540.

Describe and explain the trend from NaF to NaI and why MgCl₂ is much larger.
markscheme: Lattice enthalpy decreases from NaF to NaI (1)
The halide ion gets larger, so the ions are further apart and the attraction is weaker (1)
Mg²⁺ has double the charge of Na⁺ and is smaller, so the attraction is much stronger (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.stem:
Data: Boiling points (°C): CH₄ −162, SiH₄ −112, GeH₄ −88; NH₃ −33, PH₃ −88, AsH₃ −62.

Explain the trend in group 14 hydrides and why NH₃ does not follow the group 15 trend.
markscheme: Group 14: boiling point increases down the group (1)
More electrons, so stronger London (dispersion) forces between molecules (1)
NH₃ forms hydrogen bonds between molecules (N–H with a lone pair on N); PH₃ and AsH₃ do not, so NH₃ is anomalously high (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.stem:
Data: Chromatogram: solvent front 10.0 cm. Unknown spots at 2.5 cm and 6.0 cm. Standards: A Rf 0.25, B Rf 0.45, C Rf 0.60.

Identify the components of the unknown.
markscheme: The unknown contains A and C (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.stem:
Data: Melting points (°C): Li 180, Na 98, K 63, Rb 39.

Describe and explain the trend.
markscheme: Melting point decreases down group 1 (1)
Ionic radius increases, so the attraction between the 1+ ions and the delocalized electrons weakens (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.stem:
Data: Electronegativity data: Mg 1.3, Si 1.9, S 2.6, O 3.4.

Use the bonding triangle to compare the bonding in MgO and SiO₂ and link to one property of each.
markscheme: MgO: Δχ = 2.1, average χ = 2.35, so in the ionic region of the triangle (1)
SiO₂: Δχ = 1.5, average χ = 2.65, so polar covalent (a giant covalent network) (1)
One linked property each, e.g. MgO conducts when molten; SiO₂ has a very high melting point and does not conduct (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.topicLabel: S3.1 The periodic table: classification of elements
items.stem:
Data: First IE (kJ mol⁻¹) across period 3: Na 496, Mg 738, Al 578, Si 787, P 1012, S 1000, Cl 1251, Ar 1520.

Describe the general trend and identify the two places where it breaks.
markscheme: General increase across the period: nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell (1)
Decrease from Mg to Al: Al's outer electron is in 3p, higher in energy than 3s (1)
Decrease from P to S: S has a paired 3p electron, and the extra repulsion makes it easier to remove (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.topicLabel: S3.1 The periodic table: classification of elements
items.stem:
Data: A solution of [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ absorbs strongly near 400 nm and 700 nm and weakly in between.

Use the colour wheel to suggest the colour of the solution.
markscheme: It absorbs violet (about 400 nm) and red (about 700 nm) light (1)
It transmits the middle of the spectrum, so it appears green (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.topicLabel: S3.2 Functional groups: classification of organic compounds
items.stem:
Data: Unknown X, C₂H₄O₂. IR: very broad 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ and strong 1710 cm⁻¹. ¹H NMR: singlet at 2.1 ppm (3H), singlet at 11.5 ppm (1H).

Identify X, using the booklet IR and NMR tables.
markscheme: IR: very broad 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ is O–H in a carboxylic acid; 1710 cm⁻¹ is C=O (1)
¹H NMR: 3H singlet at 2.1 ppm is CH₃ next to C=O; 1H singlet at 11.5 ppm is the COOH proton (1)
X is ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.stem:
Data: Temperature–time data: a solution sits at 21.0 °C for 3 min, reagent added at 4 min; readings then fall steadily from 27.5 °C at 5 min to 26.0 °C at 9 min.

Explain how to find the best value of ΔT from a graph of these data.
markscheme: Extrapolate the cooling line back to the time of mixing (4 min) to correct for heat lost while the temperature was rising (1)
Maximum ≈ 27.9 °C, so ΔT ≈ 6.9 K (accept 6.8–7.0 K) rather than 6.5 K (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.stem:
Data: Born–Haber data for MgO (kJ mol⁻¹): atomisation Mg +148; IE₁ +738; IE₂ +1451; ½O=O +249; EA₁(O) −141; EA₂(O) +753; ΔHf(MgO) −602.

Calculate the lattice enthalpy of MgO and explain why EA₂ is positive.
markscheme: Lattice enthalpy = sum of the other steps − ΔHf: 148 + 738 + 1451 + 249 − 141 + 753 + 602 (1)
= +3800 kJ mol⁻¹ (compare with the data booklet value) (1)
EA₂ is endothermic: the electron is added to an O⁻ ion, which repels it (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.stem:
Data: Booklet ΔHc (kJ mol⁻¹): methanol −726 (M 32.05); ethanol −1367 (M 46.08); octane −5470 (M 114.26).

Rank the fuels by energy released per gram.
markscheme: Energy per gram = |ΔHc| ÷ M: octane 47.9, ethanol 29.7, methanol 22.7 kJ g⁻¹ (1)
Order: octane > ethanol > methanol (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
items.stem:
Data: Booklet-style data (S⦵ / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): C₂H₄(g) +220; H₂(g) +131; C₂H₆(g) +230.

Calculate ΔS⦵ for C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆ and explain its sign.
markscheme: Negative: 2 mol of gas become 1 mol of gas, so fewer ways to arrange particles and energy (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
items.stem:
Data: Titration results for 25.00 cm³ of NaOH against 0.100 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄: rough 13.1 cm³; runs 12.45, 12.50, 12.40 cm³.

Calculate the mean titre (concordant runs) and [NaOH]. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O.
markscheme: Mean of the concordant titres (rough excluded) = 12.45 cm³ (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem:
Data: Volume of CO₂ from marble chips + HCl: t/s 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150; V/cm³ 0, 28, 46, 57, 62, 62.

Describe how the rate changes and explain why it stops; estimate the average rate in the first 30 s.
markscheme: Rate decreases with time: acid concentration falls, so fewer successful collisions per second (1)
Volume stays at 62 cm³ from about 120 s because the limiting reactant is used up (1)
Average rate over the first 30 s = 28 ÷ 30 ≈ 0.93 cm³ s⁻¹ (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem:
Data: ln k against 1/T data: 1/T = 3.30 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, ln k = −5.0; 1/T = 3.10 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, ln k = −3.8.

Calculate Ea.
markscheme: Gradient = −Ea/R, so Ea = 6.0 × 10³ × 8.31 ≈ 5.0 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ = 50 kJ mol⁻¹ (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
items.stem:
Data: Equilibrium data at 700 K for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI: [H₂] = 0.010, [I₂] = 0.010, [HI] = 0.070 mol dm⁻³. A second mixture has [H₂] = 0.020, [I₂] = 0.020, [HI] = 0.10.

Calculate K and Q for the second mixture, and state the direction of change.
markscheme: Q < K, so there is a net forward reaction: more HI forms until Q = K (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.stem:
Data: pH curve: 25.0 cm³ of a weak acid titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. Start pH 2.9; pH 4.8 at 12.5 cm³; steep rise from pH 7 to 11 centred on 25.0 cm³.

Determine the concentration and pKa of the acid and choose an indicator from the booklet.
markscheme: Equivalence at 25.0 cm³ with a 1 : 1 ratio, so c(acid) = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ (1)
pKa = pH at half-equivalence (12.5 cm³) = 4.8 (1)
Phenolphthalein: its colour-change range (data booklet) lies within the steep section, pH 7–11 (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.stem:
Data: Displacement results (✓ = reaction): metal W in X²⁺(aq) ✓, in Y²⁺(aq) ✓; metal X in W²⁺(aq) ✗, in Y²⁺(aq) ✓; metal Y in W²⁺ ✗, in X²⁺ ✗.

Rank W, X and Y in order of ease of oxidation and justify.
markscheme: W displaces both other metals, X displaces only Y, Y displaces neither: a more easily oxidised metal displaces the ions of a less easily oxidised one (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.stem:
Data: Selected E⦵/V: Mg²⁺/Mg −2.37; Fe²⁺/Fe −0.45; Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34; Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36.

Identify the strongest oxidising agent and the strongest reducing agent, and the pair of half-cells giving the largest E⦵cell.
markscheme: Strongest oxidising agent: Cl₂ (most positive E⦵) (1)
Strongest reducing agent: Mg (most negative E⦵) (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.stem:
Data: Bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹, booklet): C–H 414, Cl–Cl 242, Br–Br 193.

Explain which bond UV light breaks in initiation.
markscheme: The halogen–halogen bond (Cl–Cl or Br–Br) breaks (1)
It is much weaker than C–H, so UV photons have enough energy to break it homolytically, giving radicals (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.

items.stem:
Data: Initial rate data for RBr + OH⁻: doubling [RBr] doubles the rate; doubling [OH⁻] leaves the rate unchanged.

Deduce the rate equation and whether RBr is primary or tertiary.
markscheme: Rate = k[RBr]: first order in RBr, zero order in OH⁻ (1)
OH⁻ is not in the rate-determining step, so the mechanism is SN1 and RBr is most likely tertiary (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers you use, show each step, and give units.
